meta.title: Who really said "If there is no struggle, there is no progress"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Frederick Douglass really said it, in his 1857 West India Emancipation speech at Canandaigua, New York. A verified line, public domain, only lightly re-punctuated since.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If there is no struggle, there is no progress'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Frederick Douglass, from his 1857 West India Emancipation address at Canandaigua, N.Y. Traced to the primary text and confirmed word for word.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Douglass. The line opens a famous passage from his “West India Emancipation” address, delivered at Canandaigua, New York on 3 August 1857 and first put into print that year in the pamphlet Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass. The scholarly Frederick Douglass Papers edition ↗ confirms the wording, which the original renders without the now-common comma.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “West India Emancipation” address, Canandaigua, New York
1857, in a pamphlet printed at Rochester, N.Y.

source.excerpt: Let me give you a word of the philosophy of reform. The whole history of the progress of human liberty shows that all concessions yet made to her august claims have been born of earnest struggle… If there is no struggle there is no progress. Those who profess to favor freedom and yet deprecate agitation, are men who want crops without plowing up the ground; they want rain without thunder and lightning. They want the ocean without the awful roar of its many waters… Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.
trail: The scholarly Frederick Douglass Papers Project ↗ titles the speech “The Significance of Emancipation in the West Indies,” dates it 3 August 1857, and prints the passage word for word.
The line was first put into print in the 1857 pamphlet Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass ↗, which collected the Canandaigua address alongside his speech on the Dred Scott decision.
WIST Quotations ↗ traces the exact wording to Douglass’s address at the Ontario County Agricultural Society fairgrounds in Canandaigua, New York.
source.excerptNote: The original text carries no comma—“If there is no struggle there is no progress”—and the sentence is only the opening of a longer passage that reformers still quote in full.

sourceLink.text: Read the speech at the Frederick Douglass Papers Project

source.rightsNote: Both the speech and this line were first published in 1857, long before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff, so they are firmly in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Frederick Douglass
author.heading: Frederick Douglass
author.bio: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the nineteenth century’s most celebrated Black orator, editor, and abolitionist. His autobiographies—beginning with the 1845 Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave—and his newspaper The North Star made him a defining voice for emancipation and civil rights. The 1857 Canandaigua address distilled his creed that freedom is won only through sustained struggle.

misattribution.heading: A note on the wording
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is not in dispute—this is authentically Douglass. What drifts is the wording, which circulates in trimmed and re-punctuated forms.

items.why: A compressed paraphrase widely shared on social media; Douglass’s actual sentence, per the primary text ↗, reads “If there is no struggle there is no progress.”

items.who: “If there is no struggle, there is no progress”
items.why: The popular form inserts a comma that the 1857 text does not contain—a minor edit, but worth noting for a verbatim quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the words are Douglass’s own, from the 1857 Canandaigua speech ↗; only its punctuation and length shift as it travels.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Douglass spoke at Canandaigua on the twenty-third anniversary of Britain’s emancipation of its West Indian slaves, before a crowd of more than a thousand. Four years before the Civil War, he used the occasion to argue that liberty is never granted freely—it is extracted through pressure.
The passage became the most quoted of all his orations, its logic captured in the companion line that follows: “Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.”
detailsBody: Douglass delivered the address on 3 August 1857, though when he collected it in the pamphlet Two Speeches, by Frederick Douglass he mistakenly dated the delivery to 4 August—a discrepancy that persists in some citations today.
He shared the platform with fellow abolitionists including Henry Highland Garnet, Jermain Wesley Loguen, and Austin Steward.
